common_name: Jenny Bloom Crocosmia (Golden-Yellow Montbretia with Pleated Foliage)

planting.note: Divide corm chains in early spring before growth resumes, or plant container specimens in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; Jenny Bloom bears orange buds opening to clear golden-yellow flowers in masoniorum-style horizontal heads.

directions: Jenny Bloom is a vigorous crocosmia raised by Alan Bloom in 1975, bearing orange buds that open into clear golden-yellow, tubular flowers held in compact, horizontally displayed heads reminiscent of Crocosmia masoniorum. Bloom extends from mid to late summer above strongly pleated, sword-shaped foliage that gives the clump a textured presence even before flowering begins. Plant corms in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun to partial shade, and divide congested clumps every few years in spring to maintain vigorous flowering. Its dependable yellow color and tidy habit have made it a long-standing favorite for hot-colored borders and cut-flower use.

common_name: Limpopo Crocosmia (Coral-Orange Montbretia with Golden Throat)

planting.note: Divide corm chains in early spring before growth resumes, or plant container specimens in well-drained soil in full sun; Limpopo bears wide-open coral-orange flowers with a contrasting golden throat on bronze-tinted stems.

directions: Limpopo bears wide-open, coral to salmon-orange flowers with a contrasting sunny-yellow throat, carried in dense sprays atop bronze-tinted stems from mid through late summer. The tight flower clusters open in sequence along arching spikes above clumps of erect, bright green, sword-shaped foliage, creating a long season of color. Plant corms in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun, where the warm coral tones combine well with other hot-colored perennials. The nectar-rich flowers reliably draw hummingbirds and butterflies through the height of summer.

planting.note: Divide corm chains in early spring before growth resumes, or plant container specimens in well-drained, average to fertile soil in full sun to light shade; Spitfire produces densely packed heads of orange-scarlet flowers with pale throats.

directions: Spitfire, a 1970 Alan Bloom introduction, produces densely packed heads of rich orange-scarlet flowers with pale throats, the flared blooms held tightly together along arching stems for a bold, fiery display. Flowering runs from mid to late summer above clumps of pleated, sword-like foliage typical of the genus. Grow in well-drained, average to fertile soil in full sun to light shade, and divide crowded corm clumps every three to four years to keep flower spikes strong. Its warm, saturated color pairs well with red and orange companions in a hot-themed border.

common_name: Tamar Double Red Crocosmia (Wine-Red Multi-Tepal Montbretia)

planting.note: Divide corm chains in early spring before growth resumes, or plant container specimens in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; Tamar Double Red is late-flowering with wine-red, many-tepaled blooms.

directions: Tamar Double Red, raised by Mark Wash at Trecanna Nurseries and later given the RHS Award of Garden Merit, bears rich wine-red flowers with 8 to 14 tepals rather than the usual six, giving each bloom a fuller, semi-double appearance accented by prominent yellow stamens. It is notably late flowering, beginning well after Lucifer has finished and continuing into early autumn, which extends the crocosmia season considerably. Sturdy, pleated foliage supports upright flower stems to about 1.5m that stand proud without flopping, even in exposed sites. Plant corms in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun for the strongest color and stem strength.

common_name: Paul's Best Yellow Crocosmia (Deep Golden Freesia-Like Montbretia)

planting.note: Divide corm chains in early spring before growth resumes, or plant container specimens in well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Paul's Best Yellow bears deep golden, freesia-like flowers in arching sprays.

directions: Paul's Best Yellow, an RHS Award of Garden Merit recipient, produces densely packed spikes of large, velvety, deep golden-yellow flowers with a freesia-like form, arranged in elegant arching sprays from late summer into autumn. Vigorous clumps of rich green, sword-like foliage support upright flowering stems that can reach a metre or more in height. Grow in well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade, choosing a sheltered site and mulching the corms in colder regions to protect them over winter. Its floriferous habit and long season of bloom make it well suited to swathes through a hot or tropical-themed border, and the flowers cut well for arrangements.

common_name: Castle Ward Late Crocosmia (Heirloom Reddish-Orange Starry Montbretia)

planting.note: Divide corm chains in early spring before growth resumes, or plant container specimens in moderately fertile, humus-rich soil in full sun to partial shade; Castle Ward Late is a surviving Leichtlin heirloom with reflexed, starry, reddish-orange flowers.

directions: Castle Ward Late is one of only a handful of surviving Crocosmia x crocosmioides hybrids bred by Max Leichtlin of Baden-Baden before 1895, making it a genuine heirloom still found in cultivation today. Arching stems carry an abundance of downward-facing, reddish-orange, starry flowers with reflexed petals that seem to float above the mid-green, blade-like foliage, opening from late summer through October. Grow in moderately fertile, humus-rich soil in full sun to partial shade, planting corms in groups to build the graceful, airy clumps this cultivar is known for. Its notably long bloom season and attractive seed heads make it valuable for late-season color and winter picking.

common_name: Carmin Brilliant Crocosmia (Carmine-Pink Montbretia with Golden Throat)

planting.note: Divide corm chains in early spring before growth resumes, or plant container specimens in rich, well-drained soil in full sun to light shade; Carmin Brilliant bears carmine-pink flowers with golden throats and scarlet-flushed petal reverses.

directions: Carmin Brilliant, an RHS Award of Garden Merit recipient, bears arching sprays of twenty or more carmine-pink flowers with golden-yellow throats, the reverse of each petal flushed with scarlet-orange and set off by crimson-purple calyxes and bronzy-purple stems. Bloom extends from midsummer through early fall above clumps of erect, pleated, sword-shaped green foliage. Plant corms in rich, well-drained soil in full sun to light shade, keeping soil evenly moist through the growing season for the best flower display. The unusual carmine-pink color, distinct from the more common orange and red crocosmia shades, attracts butterflies and combines well with cool-toned companions.

planting.note: Plant corms 4 inches deep in full sun after the danger of frost has passed, and stagger plantings every two weeks for a longer bloom season.

directions: Passos bears tall, robust spikes of large, ruffled florets in lavender-lilac shades splashed with deeper plum-purple near the throat, with random darker stripes along the petal edges and a hint of red for added depth. Sturdy stems can reach up to five feet, carrying single-sided flower spikes that open from the bottom up over several weeks from summer into autumn. Plant corms 4 inches deep in well-drained soil in full sun after the danger of frost has passed, staking tall spikes in exposed sites. The long, strap-like, medium green foliage is notably resistant to deer and rabbit browsing, and the profuse, richly colored blooms make excellent cut flowers.

common_name: Mon Amour Gladiolus (Soft Pastel Pink and Yellow Ruffled Gladiolus)

planting.note: Plant corms 4 inches deep in full sun once the danger of frost has passed, in rich, well-draining soil that holds enough moisture for the roots.

directions: Mon Amour produces spikes of silky, pastel blossoms that blend soft pink, pale yellow, and creamy white, with extra-large florets and softly crimped petal edges that add textural interest. Plants grow 36 to 40 inches tall and, like other large-flowering gladiolus, open their blooms from the bottom of the spike upward, giving each spike a long-lasting display of up to two weeks. Plant corms 4 inches deep in full sun after the last frost, in rich, well-draining soil that holds enough moisture for the roots. Group Mon Amour in borders, beds, or containers, and in regions colder than zone 8 lift and store corms after foliage yellows in fall.
